newsitem.title: USA: Staples CEO confident of merger approval.
newsitem.headline: Staples CEO confident of merger approval.

text.p: The CEO of Staples Inc expressed confidence Friday the Federal Trade Commission will approve his company's merger with Office Depot Inc next month, after a thorough investigation.

Thomas Stemberg, chairman and chief executive officer of Staples, said the two companies had provided "a lot of information" to the FTC and were promised an answer by the government before the end of January.
Stemberg said in a telephone interview the Canadian government decided earlier this week against standing in the way of the merger in that country.
Canadian and United States anti-trust laws are very similar, leaving the question of whether the markets in the two companies are similar.
"If anything, the market is more competitive than it is in Canada," Stemberg said. If so, that would suggest that U.S. authorities would approve the merger.

The FTC can choose to view the merger against the background of the huge market for office, supplies computer and office furniture sold in thousands of stores across the country. Or it could see the merger narrowing competition from the nation's three office superstore chains -- the third is Office Max Inc -- to two. At this point it is uncertain which way the FTC will rule.

"That is the big question," said Linda Farquhar, an associate analyst with Alex. Brown in New York. "The company would like the FTC to define the market as broadly as possible, because the products that Staples sells are widely available -- you can buy envelopes in Wal-Mart and computers in Best Buy, so why shouldn't those stores be part of the market?"

Stemberg is, of course, a strong advocate of the view that the combined forces of Staples and Office Depot -- which would be called "Staples the Office Depot" -- would together be only a small part of a large, competitive market.

"This is a highly fragmented market, which is why the entire office store industry overall does less than 10 percent share of the office products market," he said. "It's a very low share of the business."
His firm has argued to the FTC it would use the combined forces of Staples and Office Depot to lower prices.

"We will be one of the largest if not the largest buyer of office products in the world," Stemberg said, making it possible to get lower prices on items. In addition, the combined operation could lower transportation, advertising and adminstrative costs, he said.
Staples, based in Westborough, Mass., operates 473 office superstores in the United States, while Office Depot, based in Delray Beach, Fla., has 511 office superstores in the United States.
